slides.title: Course Overview: From Regression to Autocorrelation

bullets.text: This course covers simple linear regression, Gauss-Markov assumptions, and multiple regression models.
It extends to hypothesis testing, dummy variables, and handling autocorrelation in time series data.

slides.notes: Welcome to our review of Econometrics. Today we will journey from basic regression models all the way to time series issues like autocorrelation.

slides.title: Simple linear regression

bullets.text: OLS estimates minimize the sum of squared residuals: Σ(yᵢ − b₀ − b₁xᵢ)².
The slope estimate is given by b₁ = Cov(x, y) / Var(x) or Σ(xᵢ − x̄)(yᵢ − ȳ) / Σ(xᵢ − x̄)².
The slope tells us how much y changes on average when x goes up by one unit, and the residual is actual minus fitted.

slides.notes: In this section, we look at simple linear regression where we minimize the squared residuals to find our line of best fit. Remember from your probability notes that covariance and variance play a direct role in computing that slope.

slides.title: OLS assumptions (Gauss–Markov)

bullets.text: The first assumption is that the population process is linear in parameters.
MLR.5 requires homoskedasticity: Var(u | x₁, …, xₖ) = σ², meaning error variance does not depend on regressors.
Under MLR.1 to MLR.5, OLS is BLUE: the best linear unbiased estimator.
Unbiasedness needs MLR.1 through MLR.4; adding homoskedasticity gives you efficiency, making it BLUE.

slides.notes: Here we establish the Gauss-Markov assumptions. If your model satisfies assumptions 1 through 5, OLS is BLUE, meaning it is the best linear unbiased estimator.

slides.title: Multiple regression

bullets.text: β₁ measures the effect of x₁ on y holding x₂ fixed, providing the ceteris paribus interpretation.
Omitting a relevant variable that is correlated with x₁ makes our estimate b₁ biased.
The omitted variable bias is quantified as Bias(b̃₁) = β₂ · δ̃₁, where δ̃₁ comes from regressing x₂ on x₁.

slides.notes: Moving to multiple regression, we gain the power of ceteris paribus interpretation. Be very careful with omitted variables, as leaving them out when they are correlated with your regressors introduces direct bias.

slides.title: Hypothesis testing: t and F

bullets.text: The t-test statistic is the estimate divided by its standard error, compared to a t distribution with n − 2 degrees of freedom.
An F test asks: if I force these coefficients to zero, how much worse does the fit get?
You can test multiple restrictions like H₀: β₂ = β₃ = 0 using the F statistic derived from restricted and unrestricted R².

slides.notes: For hypothesis testing, we use t-tests for individual coefficients and F-tests when we want to test multiple restrictions simultaneously. Think of the F-test as measuring how much worse the model fit becomes when you drop those variables.

slides.title: Dummy variables and interactions

bullets.text: An interaction term lets the effect of one variable on the outcome depend on the value of another variable.
When including categorical groups with an intercept, include g − 1 dummies for g groups.
Including all g dummy variables creates perfect collinearity, known as the dummy variable trap.

slides.notes: Dummy variables let us handle qualitative factors. Always remember to drop one category to avoid the dummy variable trap of perfect collinearity, and use interaction terms when effects depend on other factors.

slides.title: Autocorrelation

bullets.text: Autocorrelation means that the error in this period is correlated with the error in the previous period.
With AR(1) errors where uₜ = ρuₜ₋₁ + eₜ, OLS remains unbiased but the usual standard errors are invalid.
The Durbin–Watson statistic d ≈ 2(1 − ρ̂) helps detect this, where values near 2 indicate no first-order autocorrelation.

slides.notes: In time series models, autocorrelation occurs when current errors correlate with past errors. While OLS stays unbiased under AR(1) errors, standard errors break down, so we look to metrics like the Durbin-Watson statistic.

slides.title: Key takeaways

bullets.text: OLS minimizes squared residuals, and under Gauss-Markov assumptions (including homoskedasticity), it is BLUE.
Multiple regression enables ceteris paribus analysis, but omitted variables create bias tied to underlying regressions.
Watch out for structural pitfalls like the dummy variable trap and temporal issues like autocorrelation in time series.

slides.notes: To wrap up for your exam: master the mechanics of OLS, keep Gauss-Markov assumptions and omitted variable bias straight, and remember how to handle dummy traps and autocorrelation.
